name: Battleship Grey
lede: Battleship Grey is a name for use, not for nature: the grey in which warships were painted, recorded as a color from 1912 and now a near-neutral mid grey on screens.

sections.title: A name from use
sections.body:
Paterson defines battleship grey as the bluish grey in which battleships are often painted [1]. Garfield, reporting Judd's count of 7,500 color names, lists battleship grey among 59 end-use names [2]. Our library traces the name to Ridgway's 1912 atlas, with later entries in RAL (1927), Maerz and Paul (1930), ISCC-NBS (1955) and the xkcd survey (2010) [3]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1910s [4].

Ball links the paint to a mineral: barium sulphate, commonly used as a cheap extender in white pigments, went into the US Navy's paint called Battleship Grey, starting in the 1910s [5].

sections.title: Where it turns up
sections.body: St Clair tells of a red car in a Turin museum that fell into a Genoese dock after an American motor show and was repainted, to stop rust, with the only paint to hand, tins of battleship gray; it is now dull grey [6]. Finlay borrows the word for a different grey, the volcanic basalt of the San Carlos mesa [7]. Both uses show how far it traveled from the navy: it became a shorthand for flat, practical grey.

sections.title: Swatch against name
sections.body: The swatch is nearly neutral (lightness 55, chroma 1), while Paterson's definition says bluish [1][3]. The xkcd survey's version, #6B7C85, is the bluer one, closer to the dictionary meaning [3]. The swatch matches other neutral names to within a few units, including old silver and Pearl Light Grey [3]. In plain words it is a mid [[grey]], between [[light-grey]] and [[dark-grey]], and bluer relatives such as [[steel-grey]] and [[slate-grey]] sit nearby.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
The hue is present in 566 of 23,781 paintings (2.38 per cent), more than 77 per cent of the named colors, and in a painting it is most often a mid-tone (42 per cent of 309) [8]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 42 of 1,674 paintings, 1.7 times the baseline [8]. The painter most devoted to it is [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]], in 6 of 50 works here, 4.6 times the baseline [8]. It shares canvases with [[blackish-grey]] and dark grey more than chance [8].

The earliest match dates to 1278, 634 years before the name's first record in 1912 [3][8]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a navy-paint test [8].
